case.dispatchHook: Everglades energy monitor says a heron feeds the sawgrass. Fix the arrows.
briefing: Agent, the energy monitor at an Everglades field station has its arrows pointing backward.
According to the screen, a heron feeds the sawgrass and the Sun runs on frogs.
Rebuild the food chain, then check the adaptation files the same glitch touched.
The herons are fine. The monitor is not.

lab.intro: The energy log for one Everglades food chain came back shuffled. Put the links back in the order energy moves.
lab.prompt: Put the food chain in order, starting where the energy comes from.

steps.name: Sun
steps.card: Gives off the light that starts the chain

steps.name: Sawgrass
steps.card: Uses sunlight to make its own food

steps.name: Heron
steps.card: Wades in the marsh and eats frogs

lab.why: Energy starts with the Sun, goes to sawgrass (the producer), and then moves to each consumer that eats the one before it.

case.debriefClosed: Case closed. Energy flows from the Sun again, at least on the monitor. Log it.
case.debriefOpen: Case stays open for now. Keep your field binoculars ready; the swamp predators are still on the hunt.

items.stem: An osprey dives into a Florida lake and grabs a fish with its feet. Then it tears the fish into small pieces to eat. Which beak shape best helps the osprey tear meat?
options: short, cone-shaped beak
long, thin beak
flat, wide beak
sharp, hooked beak
why: Decoy: a short, cone-shaped beak is best for cracking hard seeds.
Decoy: a long, thin beak is best for spearing or probing, like a heron's.
Decoy: a flat, wide beak is best for scooping or straining food from water, like a duck's.
Correct: a sharp, hooked beak can grip and tear meat, so it fits a bird that eats fish.
keyWords: tears the fish into small pieces
items.alt: Three bird heads: one with a long, thin beak, one with a hooked beak, and one with a short, cone-shaped beak, each beside the food it takes.
items.tisCheck: Physical adaptation (beak shape matched to food) for a Florida bird; SC.5.L.17.1 limits are UNVERIFIED, so the item stays with plain structure and function.
items.misconceptions: Any strong beak works for any food; beak shape is unrelated to diet.

items.stem: A brown pelican and a barred owl both live in Florida. The pelican has webbed feet. The owl has sharp, curved claws. Which statement best explains why their feet are different?
options: The pelican's feet became webbed because it swam a lot when it was young.
Each bird's feet fit how it lives: the pelican paddles on water, and the owl grabs its prey.
Both kinds of feet mainly help the birds stay warm on cold nights.
The pelican's feet help it grip branches, and the owl's claws help it swim.
why: Decoy: webbed feet are inherited, and swimming practice does not grow skin between the toes.
Correct: webbed feet push against water like paddles, and sharp claws hold prey, so each fits the bird's way of life.
Decoy: neither kind of foot is mainly for warmth, because each shape matches how the bird moves or feeds.
Decoy: the jobs are swapped, because webbing helps a bird swim and claws help it grip.
items.alt: A brown pelican and a barred owl shown side by side.
items.tisCheck: Physical adaptations of Florida birds (feet matched to how they move and feed); SC.5.L.17.1 limits are UNVERIFIED, so no evolution or natural selection terms.
items.misconceptions: Body parts change from use during one lifetime; adaptations are mainly about temperature; structure and job mixed up.

items.stem: Rangers at a Florida wildlife refuge counted American white pelicans on the same lake in different months. Their counts are in the table. Which explanation best fits the data?
options: The pelicans migrate to Florida for its mild winters, then fly north to nest in summer.
The pelicans hibernate in the lake mud during the hot summer months.
The pelicans leave Florida in winter because the lake freezes over.
The pelicans all die each summer, and new ones hatch on the lake each winter.
why: Correct: the counts are high in the cool months and zero in July, which fits birds that spend winter in Florida and nest farther north.
Decoy: birds do not hibernate in mud, and the pelicans were not on the lake to be counted in July.
Decoy: this is backward, because the pelicans are on the lake in winter, and Florida lakes do not freeze over.
Decoy: young pelicans could not hatch and be full grown in a few months, so the same birds are returning.
items.alt: A table of pelican counts: January 140, April 20, July 0, October 60, December 130.
items.tisCheck: Seasonal behavior in Florida compared with other regions (SC.4.L.17.1, also assessed with SC.5.L.17.1); counts are only compared, no computation.
items.misconceptions: Birds hibernate; Florida winters are harsh; animals that disappear for a season have died.

items.stem: Flamingos live in parts of South Florida. The table compares adult flamingos that eat three different diets. Which trait is changed mostly by the flamingo's environment?
options: its long legs, because they help it wade
its bent bill, because it uses the bill to strain food
its feather color, because it depends on the food it eats
all of its traits, because every trait comes from the environment
why: Decoy: every adult in the table has long legs, so leg length is inherited and does not change with diet.
Decoy: every adult in the table has a bent bill, so bill shape is inherited.
Correct: feather color changes with the food each flamingo eats, so the environment affects it.
Decoy: legs and bills stay the same with every diet, so not every trait comes from the environment.
keyWords: changed mostly by the flamingo's environment

visual.title: Adult Flamingo Notes
rows: Zoo food with no shrimp or algae
Zoo food with color from shrimp added

items.alt: A table comparing three adult flamingos on different diets: feather color changes, while long legs and a bent bill stay the same.
items.tisCheck: Inherited traits vs traits affected by the environment (SC.4.L.16.2, also assessed with SC.5.L.17.1); no genes or DNA terms.
items.misconceptions: Useful traits are caused by the environment; every trait is either all inherited or all environmental.

items.stem: Each answer choice describes an animal behavior. Which behavior is learned and not inherited?
options: A sea turtle hatchling crawls toward the ocean right after it hatches.
A garden spider spins a web the first time it tries.
A dog sits when its owner says the word sit.
A barred owl chick calls for food when a parent lands at the nest.
why: Decoy: no one shows the hatchling the way, so this behavior is inherited.
Decoy: the spider builds a web without being taught, so this behavior is inherited.
Correct: a dog has to be taught to sit on command, so this behavior is learned.
Decoy: chicks call for food without being taught, so this behavior is inherited.
items.alt: A dog and her puppy with the same coat pattern, and the puppy learning to sit on command.
items.tisCheck: Inherited vs learned behavior (SC.4.L.16.3, also assessed with SC.5.L.17.1); Florida animals and a pet, no genetics terms.
items.misconceptions: Any skilled behavior must be learned; behaviors done by young animals are learned from parents.

items.stem: People drain half of a wetland near the Everglades and fill it with dirt to build a road. Herons that hunted fish and frogs on that side lose their feeding area. What will most likely happen to these herons?
options: Many will move to other wetlands to find food, and fewer will live in this area.
They will grow shorter legs so they can live on the dry land.
Nothing will change, because birds can fly over the road.
They will hunt on the dry side, because fish are easier to catch there.
why: Correct: when people change a habitat, animals that lose their food must move or fewer of them survive there.
Decoy: a heron cannot change its body to fit a new environment during its life.
Decoy: flying over the road does not bring back the fish and frogs that lived in the drained wetland.
Decoy: fish and frogs need water, so they will not be on the dry side.
items.alt: A wetland half drained for a road, with wading birds on the wet side and a bulldozer on the dry side.
items.tisCheck: How people change an environment and how animals respond (SC.4.L.17.4, also assessed with SC.5.L.17.1); no extinction data or computation.
items.misconceptions: Animals change their bodies to fit a new place; flying animals are never affected by habitat loss.

items.stem: The diagram shows a food chain from the Everglades. What do the arrows in the food chain show?
options: which living thing is bigger than the next one
the order in which the living things were born
the direction energy moves, from the food to the eater
which animal eats the living thing the arrow points to
why: Decoy: size is not what the arrows show, since some eaters are smaller than their food.
Decoy: the arrows show energy moving, not when each living thing was born.
Correct: each arrow points from the food to the living thing that eats it, showing where the energy goes.
Decoy: this is backward, because the arrow points to the eater, not to the food.
items.alt: A food chain in a row with arrows: Sun, sawgrass, grasshopper, frog, heron.
items.tisCheck: Energy flow shown by food chain arrows (SC.4.L.17.3); SC.4.L.17.3 limits are UNVERIFIED, so a single Florida chain with no energy amounts.
items.misconceptions: Arrows point from the eater to what it eats; arrows show size or order of birth.

items.stem: The diagram shows part of a food web in the Indian River Lagoon. Which living thing in this web makes its own food using energy from sunlight?
options: shrimp
sea grass
blue crab
brown pelican
why: Decoy: shrimp are small and low in the web, but they eat other living things, so they are consumers.
Correct: sea grass is a producer that uses energy from sunlight to make its own food.
Decoy: a blue crab eats other living things, so it is a consumer.
Decoy: a brown pelican eats fish, so it is a consumer at the top of this web.
items.alt: A food web in which sea grass and algae feed a shrimp, a crab, and a small fish, which feed a larger fish and a pelican.
items.tisCheck: Producers make food from sunlight and consumers eat (SC.4.L.17.2, also assessed with SC.4.L.17.3); food web as a stimulus only.
items.misconceptions: The smallest living thing is the producer; animals near the bottom of a web make food; water animals get energy straight from the Sun.

items.stem: In this lagoon food web, shrimp, crabs, and small fish eat sea grass and algae. Pelicans eat the small fish. Suppose a disease kills most of the sea grass. Which change will most likely happen?
options: The pelicans will not be affected, because they do not eat sea grass.
The shrimp will start making their own food using sunlight.
There will be more small fish, because the sea grass is no longer in the way.
There will be fewer small fish, so the pelicans will have less food.
why: Decoy: pelicans eat fish that eat sea grass, so losing the sea grass reaches them too.
Decoy: animals cannot make their own food, even when their food runs short.
Decoy: small fish depend on sea grass for food, so losing it means fewer small fish, not more.
Correct: the small fish lose much of their food, so there are fewer of them, and the pelicans that eat them have less food.
keyWords: kills most of the sea grass
items.alt: A food web in which sea grass and algae feed a shrimp, a crab, and a small fish, which feed a larger fish and a pelican.
items.tisCheck: What happens along a food web when a producer is lost (SC.4.L.17.3); limits are UNVERIFIED, so changes are described in words with no numbers.
items.misconceptions: Only animals that eat a plant directly are affected when it disappears; animals can switch to making food.

items.stem: In a Florida forest, a live oak uses sunlight to make food. White-tailed deer eat its leaves and acorns. A Florida panther hunts the deer. Which list shows the path of energy in order?
options: Sun, live oak, deer, panther
panther, deer, live oak, Sun
Sun, deer, live oak, panther
live oak, Sun, deer, panther
why: Correct: energy goes from the Sun to the live oak (the producer), then to the deer that eats it, then to the panther.
Decoy: this list runs backward, from the top consumer to the Sun.
Decoy: a deer cannot get energy straight from the Sun, so it must come after the live oak.
Decoy: the Sun is where the energy starts, so it comes before the live oak.
items.alt: A Florida panther, the hunter at the end of this food chain.
items.tisCheck: Energy flows from the Sun through producers to consumers in a Florida food chain (SC.4.L.17.3); order only, no energy amounts.
items.misconceptions: Food chains start with the biggest animal; animals get energy straight from the Sun; the producer comes before the Sun.

items.stem: A manatee eats sea grass for many hours each day. The sea grass does not eat anything. How does the sea grass get the energy it needs to live and grow?
options: It takes in food from the mud through its roots.
It catches tiny animals that float in the water.
It gets energy from the manatees that eat it.
It makes its own food using energy from sunlight.
why: Decoy: roots take in water and nutrients, but they do not take in food.
Decoy: sea grass is a plant, and it does not catch or eat animals.
Decoy: energy moves from the sea grass to the manatee, not the other way.
Correct: sea grass is a producer, so it makes its own food using energy from sunlight.
keyWords: sea grass does not eat anything
items.alt: A manatee swimming in clear water.
items.tisCheck: Plants make their own food from sunlight and animals cannot (SC.4.L.17.2, also assessed with SC.4.L.17.3); no photosynthesis vocabulary.
items.misconceptions: Plants get food from soil or mud; energy flows from the eater back to the food.

items.stem: A class made a table of what living things eat at a Florida pond. Suppose a disease killed most of the grasshoppers. What would most likely happen to the grass?
options: There would be less grass, because grass gets its energy from grasshoppers.
There would be more grass, because fewer animals would be eating it.
The grass would start eating insects to replace the grasshoppers.
The grass would not change, because plants are not part of food chains.
why: Decoy: energy moves from the grass to the grasshoppers, not the other way.
Correct: with fewer grasshoppers eating it, more of the grass would be left to grow.
Decoy: grass is a producer that makes its own food, so it cannot eat insects.
Decoy: plants are the producers that start food chains, so they are part of them.

visual.title: Who Eats What at the Pond
rows: Nothing. It makes its own food using sunlight.

items.alt: A table: grass makes its own food, grasshoppers eat grass, green tree frogs eat grasshoppers and other insects, and largemouth bass eat frogs and small fish.
items.tisCheck: Effect on a producer when a consumer that eats it disappears (SC.4.L.17.3); limits are UNVERIFIED, so changes are described in words with no numbers.
items.misconceptions: Energy flows from consumers back to producers; plants are not part of food chains; producers can switch to eating.

codex.title: The Sun
codex.line: Almost all the energy in a food chain starts as sunlight.

codex.title: Sawgrass
codex.line: This Everglades producer has tiny sharp teeth along the edges of its blades.

codex.title: Heron
codex.line: Herons wade on long legs and catch fish and frogs with long, sharp beaks.
